verdicts.rewritten_summary: Encyclopaedic national-rights page containing Santa Catarina-specific entries: the state's constitution (anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002) lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds but, as of 2019, does not address discrimination against transgender people; from 2020 people in Santa Catarina obtain documents recording non-binary gender judicially or through notarial offices even though no specific law prescribes it; in Florianópolis, judge M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva of the 1st Civil Court blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. National framework claimed by the record: same-sex marriage legal nationwide since 2013 (CNJ Resolution 175/2013) and the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling making discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation/gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989.

Outright International country page: constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions following the 2019 Supreme Court ruling prohibit discrimination and hate crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity, yet a deeply conservative Congress has generated a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. In September 2025 the government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee (a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019) for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy, and the Superior Court of Justice ruled nonbinary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity. National-framework source kept per rule 5: the record claims nationwide legal protections identical for this state's visitors and no region-specific source covers that claim.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Law-firm guide for expats, updated 5 April 2026: names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name/gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction though legal rights are identical nationwide. Foreign same-sex spouses and partners are treated identically for visa and residence categories (spousal residence permit), foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes, joint and second-parent adoption are confirmed (STF RE 846.102, 2015), gender-marker changes proceed without surgery, and the STF's ADO 26 (2019) criminalises homophobia and transphobia as equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989.

Statistics Canada 'The Daily' release (30 March 2026) on police-reported hate crime in Canada, 2024: 4,882 hate crimes reported, +1% from 2023 (which had risen 34% from 2022), more than doubling (+169%) since 2018; the rate per 100,000 population fell 2% to 11.9 incidents. Incidents targeting sexual orientation declined 26% to 658, while religion-motivated incidents were essentially stable at 1,342. No British Columbia-specific figures appear in the release (national context only).

verdicts.rewritten_summary: Outright International country page (12 March 2026): same-sex marriage and adoption legal since March 2022; since 2012 Chile's hate-crime law has included sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances and same-sex civil unions have been recognised since 2015; a 2019 comprehensive legal gender-recognition law is based on self-determination, and a third sex option has been available for intersex children on birth certificates since 2006. No legal ban exists on medically unnecessary interventions on minors, though the Health Minister published non-binding intersex-affirming guidance in 2023; a 2020 family-court decision recognised two women as parents of a child born through assisted reproduction and a 2025 criminal court issued the country's first conviction in the field. National-framework source kept per rule 5: the record claims the national score and no region-specific source covers the national framework this pass.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: El País English (14 April 2025), reporting from Bello, Antioquia: 32-year-old trans woman Sara Millerey González Borja was beaten and thrown into a waterway in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; the video went viral on 5 April, President Gustavo Petro ordered an investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025 (the first two victims were gay men); a clinic reportedly did not treat her as an emergency 'because she didn't get shot', and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. The article records 13 trans people killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone and notes city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

The Guardian (30 July 2024), reporting from Caquetá: more than 40 transgender women were killed in Colombia in 2023 (41 recorded) and eight more between February and April 2024; armed groups circulating in Caquetá - where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement - distributed flyers on streets and WhatsApp announcing a 'social cleansing' plan naming 'faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes' as legitimate military targets, and trans women there were forced to flee after death threats. Retained per rule 5: this supports the record's national-frame claims (2023-24 kill tallies and the southern-department social-cleansing flyers) and no region-specific Antioquia source covers them.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: BuzzFeed investigation posted 12 January 2018: under Article D248 of the criminal-procedure code men and women must be held in separate establishments, but placement follows the legal gender on identity documents, so trans women still recorded as male are held in all-male facilities - the group that, per controller-general Adeline Hazan, 'suffers the most' in prison. Region-relevant case: Paola, transferred in 2014 to Lille's northern correctional facility, was met by detainees shouting 'We don't want any women here!', a fellow inmate tried to attack her with a knife and she spent two days in solitary confinement; Kara B. was held under conditions described as worrying after her 2016 Paris protest trial; the Ministry of Justice counted 13 transgender detainees across eight facilities as of 1 November 2016.

National detention-oversight opinion of 25 May 2021 (covering every place of deprivation of liberty; prepared from referrals received since 2010 concerning transgender detainees): assignment to establishments or wards (male or female) is based exclusively on civil status, so the vast majority of transgender people are held in institutions or wards that do not correspond to their gender identity, and search procedures for persons whose civil-status sex does not match their identity add constraints such as isolation. It recommends guaranteeing every transgender detainee the possibility of choosing the sex of searching officers and of their ward, bars identity-based isolation, requires continuity of medical and hormone care with free choice of doctor, urges research funding, and faults the administration for not translating the 2016 justice-modernisation law (n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016) into prison rules.
verdicts.note: national-framework source; rule-5 retention: record text claims the May 2021 opinion and no region-specific source covers it
